label: Figure 7
title: What pay transparency and salary-history rules did to pay, in the studies that measured it
caption: Five measured effects of transparency and salary-history rules. Right-to-discuss laws lowered wages by about 2 percent [90](#cite:90); posting laws raised disclosure by about 30 percentage points and wages by 1.3 to 3.6 percent with no change in employment [97](#cite:97); salary-history bans raised the gender earnings ratio by about 1 percent, driven by job changers [96](#cite:96); told where they stood, below-median earners at one employer grew less satisfied and looked for work while above-median earners did not change [92](#cite:92). The review that frames them says the effect depends on which kind of transparency a rule creates [91](#cite:91).
how_to_read: Read the policy column first: these are different rules with different mechanisms, and the findings do not add up to one number. The population column says where the result was measured; a result from one employer is a result from one employer. The design column is the evidence grade the guide uses.

explain.text: Laws protecting workers who ask about coworkers' pay; the wage effect is muted where workers have little individual bargaining power [90](#cite:90).
A requirement to state the range in the advertisement, the rule the state overlay tracks [97](#cite:97).

source: Findings are quoted as the pack recorded them from each study's reported results [90](#cite:90) [91](#cite:91) [92](#cite:92) [96](#cite:96) [97](#cite:97); no pooling, no conversion.
